title: Why does a linear least squares fit appear to have a bias when applied to simple test data?
attempt: Ordinary least squares (OLS) minimizes the sum of squared VERTICAL residuals (in the y-direction). When you regress y on x, OLS finds the line that best predicts y from x, which is not the same as the line that best fits the data in a geometric (orthogonal) sense. The covariance eigenvector points in the direction of maximum variance, which minimizes ORTHOGONAL (perpendicular) distances to the line. These are different criteria: OLS assumes all the error is in y and x is measured without error; the PCA/covariance direction treats x and y symmetrically. When the data are correlated, the OLS slope (which equals r*sy/sx) is always shallower than the eigenvector direction, which is why the OLS fit looks 'tilted' relative to the direction of maximum variance. This is not a bias in OLS; it is the intended behavior of minimizing vertical errors. The apparent tilt is the difference between regressing y-on-x (predicting y) and the symmetric principal-component direction.

title: Why do some LLMs like ChatGPT add random words in foreign languages?
attempt: This happens because of how tokenization works in multilingual models. LLMs are trained on text from many languages, and their tokenizer (e.g., BPE) splits text into subword units that span multiple languages. When the model generates text, it predicts the next token from this mixed vocabulary. Occasionally, a token from another language gets a high probability, especially if the training data had code-switching, loanwords, or if the context resembles text in another language. The 'random' foreign words are tokens the model assigns non-trivial probability to, not a deliberate choice. It is a known artifact of multilingual training and byte-level tokenization, where the boundary between languages is not hard-coded into the model.

title: Why are so many problems linear and how would one solve nonlinear problems?
attempt: Many problems are approximately linear because (a) linear models are the first-order Taylor approximation of any smooth function near a point, so locally most relationships look linear; (b) linear models are tractable, interpretable, and have closed-form solutions, so they are the default starting point; (c) many physical laws are linear or linearizable. For nonlinear problems, approaches include: (1) feature engineering, transforming inputs (polynomials, logs, interactions) and still using linear regression; (2) nonlinear models, neural networks, kernel methods, tree-based models (random forests, gradient boosting), generalized additive models (GAMs); (3) local linear methods, fitting linear models locally (loess, kernel regression). The choice depends on the data size, interpretability needs, and the nature of the nonlinearity.

title: Is there any problem with too much (or false) precision?
attempt: False precision (more decimals than the measurement supports) is mostly a cosmetic and communication issue rather than a statistical one. It can mislead readers into thinking the data are more accurate than they are. For ages, storing 0.001 years (sub-day resolution) when the underlying data are in days implies false accuracy. However, for infants where day-level resolution matters, the extra decimals are still harmless because they arise from a deterministic conversion (days/365.25). The real risk is when false precision is interpreted as real precision, for example in meta-analyses that weight by inverse variance, or when small differences are treated as meaningful. The fix is to round to the resolution the measurement actually supports, not to avoid decimal arithmetic.

title: Is body mass index (BMI) actually the interaction term for weight x height^-2?
attempt: BMI = weight/height^2 is a ratio, and statistically it acts like an interaction (product) between weight and height^-2. In a regression of an outcome on weight and height, including weight*height^-2 (or equivalently weight/height^2) as a predictor is a specific functional-form assumption: it says the effect of weight on the outcome depends on height in exactly this inverse-square way. This is a strong assumption. The textbook recommendation to include both main effects (weight and height) plus their interaction is more flexible, it lets the data determine how weight and height combine, rather than imposing the exact BMI form. So BMI is a particular constrained interaction term, not the general interaction. Whether it is appropriate depends on whether the inverse-square relationship is substantively justified.

title: What is the connection between measure theory and statistics?
attempt: Measure theory provides the rigorous foundation for probability. In measure theory, a probability space is a measure space where the total measure is 1. A random variable is a measurable function from the sample space to the real numbers. The distribution of a random variable is the pushforward measure. Expectation is the integral with respect to the probability measure. This foundation matters for statistics because: (1) it unifies discrete and continuous distributions (both are just measures); (2) it makes rigorous concepts like conditional expectation (Radon-Nikodym derivative), almost-sure convergence, and the law of large numbers; (3) it handles pathological cases (non-existent densities, singular distributions) that arise in advanced theory. For applied work, you do not need the measure-theoretic details, but the framework guarantees that the probability calculations are well-defined.

title: Is Backpropagation faulty?
attempt: No, backpropagation is not faulty. The apparent issue is a misunderstanding of what the gradient computation does. When we update the weights in layer 1, the forward pass that produced the activations for layer 2 is recomputed with the new weights. The backpropagation algorithm computes the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight via the chain rule, and this computation is exact for the current parameter values. The concern that 'updating layer 1 changes the input to layer 2, so the gradient is no longer correct' is about the fact that the gradient is evaluated at a specific point in parameter space. In gradient descent, we compute the gradient at the current point and take a small step; we do not need the gradient to remain valid after the step, we recompute it at the new point. This is true of all gradient-based optimization, not specific to backpropagation.

title: How to interpret a p-value when 0.01 < p < 0.05
attempt: A p-value between 0.01 and 0.05 means that, assuming the null hypothesis is true, the probability of observing a result as extreme as (or more extreme than) the one obtained is between 1% and 5%. Whether this is 'significant' depends on the chosen significance level (alpha). If alpha=0.05, then p<0.05 is conventionally called 'statistically significant', but p=0.049 and p=0.051 are essentially the same strength of evidence, and the 0.05 threshold is arbitrary. The p-value is NOT the probability that the null hypothesis is true, nor the probability that the result is due to chance. It is the probability of the data (or more extreme) given the null. A p-value in this range is modest evidence against the null, but it should be interpreted alongside effect size, confidence intervals, and the study design, not as a binary significant/not-significant verdict.

title: The standard deviation is the statistical measure that describes, on average, how far each data point is from the mean
attempt: The statement is imprecise but captures an intuition. The standard deviation is the square root of the average squared deviation from the mean, not the average absolute deviation. The measure that IS the average distance from the mean is the mean absolute deviation (MAD). The standard deviation weights larger deviations more heavily (because it squares them), so it is more sensitive to outliers than the MAD. The statement is popular because the standard deviation is the most widely used measure of spread and has nice mathematical properties (it is the natural parameter of the normal distribution, it is additive for independent variables). A more accurate informal description: the standard deviation measures spread around the mean, giving more weight to points farther from the mean, and it is the typical distance in the sense of the root-mean-square deviation.

title: When to use which formula for sample variance?
attempt: The two formulas are: (1) s^2 = sum((xi - xbar)^2)/(n-1), the definition, using deviations from the sample mean; (2) s^2 = (sum(xi^2) - n*xbar^2)/(n-1), the computational formula, using the sum of squares minus the correction term. They are algebraically identical. You use formula (1) when you want to emphasize the definition or when you are reasoning about the concept. You use formula (2) for hand computation or when the raw sum of squares is already available, because it avoids computing each deviation separately. The reason they might give different answers in practice is catastrophic cancellation: if the mean is large relative to the deviations, sum(xi^2) and n*xbar^2 are both large and nearly equal, so subtracting them loses precision. In that case, formula (1) or a two-pass algorithm is more numerically stable.

title: Is it always valid to use correlation for feature selection?
attempt: No, correlation-based feature selection has important limitations. (1) Correlation measures only linear association, so a feature with a strong nonlinear relationship to the target can have near-zero correlation and be wrongly discarded. (2) Correlation does not account for interactions, so a feature may be useless alone but powerful in combination with others. (3) Correlation with the target does not imply the feature adds predictive value in a multivariate model (it may be redundant with other features). For tree-based models (which capture nonlinearities and interactions), low correlation does NOT mean the feature is unhelpful. A safer approach is to use model-based importance (e.g., from a random forest or gradient boosting) or to test the feature's incremental value in the actual model, rather than relying on marginal correlation alone.

title: Are p-values still useful even though errors are not normal?
attempt: Yes, p-values remain useful even when normality assumptions are violated, for several reasons. (1) Many tests are robust to non-normality, especially with moderate to large samples, thanks to the central limit theorem, the sampling distribution of the test statistic (e.g., the t-statistic for a mean) is approximately normal even when the raw data are not. (2) For regression, the normality assumption that matters most is for the validity of t-tests and F-tests on coefficients; with large samples, these are approximately valid even with non-normal errors (asymptotic theory). (3) Bootstrap and permutation methods give p-values without normality assumptions. The key is to check whether the sample size is large enough for asymptotic approximations to hold, and to use robust methods (robust standard errors, bootstrap) when in doubt. P-values are a tool; their validity depends on the context, not on a blanket normality requirement.

title: Bertrand's Box Paradox
attempt: The answer is 1/3, not 50%. There are three boxes: GG (two gold), SS (two silver), GS (one gold, one silver). You pick a box at random and draw a gold ball. Given that you drew gold, the box cannot be SS. It is either GG or GS, but these are NOT equally likely. There are 3 gold balls in total (2 in GG, 1 in GS). Given you drew a gold ball, the probability it came from GG is 2/3 (because 2 of the 3 gold balls are in GG), and from GS is 1/3. If the box is GG, the other ball is gold. If the box is GS, the other ball is silver. So P(other is silver | drew gold) = P(box is GS | drew gold) = 1/3. The answer is 1/3, not 1/2, because the gold ball you drew is more likely to have come from the GG box.

title: Is it possible to perform a statistical analysis with only one experimental unit per group if I know the variance?
attempt: Yes, if you truly know the population variance (sigma^2), you can perform a comparison of means with one observation per group using a z-test. With one observation per group and known sigma, the difference in means has a normal distribution with variance sigma^2*(1/n1 + 1/n2) = 2*sigma^2 (if n1=n2=1). You can construct a confidence interval and test for a difference. The catch is that 'knowing the variance' is a strong assumption. In practice, variance is estimated from data, and with one observation per group you cannot estimate within-group variance. If the known variance is reliable (from prior studies or physical theory), a z-test is valid. If the variance is estimated or uncertain, you have no way to assess within-group variability with n=1 per group, and no frequentist test is possible.

title: Why include unadjusted estimates in a study when reporting adjusted estimates?
attempt: Unadjusted (crude) estimates and adjusted estimates answer different questions, and both are informative. The unadjusted estimate is the raw association between exposure and outcome, without controlling for any confounders. The adjusted estimate is the association after controlling for confounders. Reporting both serves several purposes: (1) the unadjusted estimate is what would be observed in the population without intervention, which is relevant for public-health impact; (2) the difference between unadjusted and adjusted estimates reveals the magnitude of confounding; (3) transparency, readers can see how much the estimate changes when confounders are controlled. The STROBE guideline recommends both because the crude estimate is often the more policy-relevant number, while the adjusted estimate is the more causally-interpretable one. Neither is 'correct', they answer different questions.

title: Can sample size be considered a statistic?
attempt: This depends on the definition of 'statistic.' By the formal definition, a statistic is any function of the sample data, so sample size n IS a statistic, because n = T(X1,...,Xn) counts the observations, which is a function of the sample. However, n is a degenerate statistic: it does not vary with the values of the data, only with how many observations were collected. In practice, n is usually treated as a fixed design parameter rather than a random variable, because the sample size is chosen by the researcher (not random). Under Bluman's definition (a characteristic computed from sample values), n qualifies. Under the stricter definition (a function used to estimate a population parameter), n does not qualify because it estimates nothing. The answer is: yes by the formal definition, but it is a degenerate case that is usually treated as a known constant.

title: How to quantify the systematic error in linear regression fit?
attempt: Systematic error (bias) in a regression fit refers to systematic deviations between the observed and predicted values that the model's structure cannot capture, e.g., a nonlinear true relationship fit with a linear model. To quantify it: (1) examine the residuals vs fitted plot, a systematic pattern (e.g., a U-shape) indicates unmodeled structure; (2) the mean of the residuals within regions of the fitted values, systematic non-zero means indicate bias; (3) compare the model's predictions to a more flexible fit (e.g., a GAM or a higher-order polynomial), the discrepancy is an estimate of the systematic error; (4) lack-of-fit test (if you have replicates), compares the pure error to the residual error. The covariance matrix of the coefficients quantifies the STATISTICAL error (variance from sampling), but systematic error is about model misspecification, which requires examining the residuals' structure.

title: Does it matter if the correlation coefficient is closer to 0 than 1?
attempt: Yes, it matters for interpretation. A correlation of 0.428 (closer to 0 than to 1) indicates a weak-to-moderate linear association, not a strong one. The mark scheme's point is that 0.428 is far from 1, so it does not represent a strong correlation. Whether 0.428 is 'significant' depends on the sample size. With n=10, the critical value for significance at alpha=0.05 is about 0.56, so 0.428 is NOT statistically significant (it is within the range of sampling variation under the null of no correlation). The 'closer to 0 than to 1' language is a heuristic to remind students that 0.428 is a weak correlation, not a strong one. Both points in the mark scheme are correct: the correlation is weak (closer to 0) and not significant at n=10.

title: Why does classical testing privilege Type I error (vs. the symmetric Bayesian view)?
attempt: Classical (Neyman-Pearson) hypothesis testing privileges Type I error because of its asymmetric decision framework. In NP theory, you fix the Type I error rate (alpha) at a small value (e.g., 0.05) and then minimize the Type II error (beta) subject to that constraint. The null hypothesis is given a special status: you 'reject' or 'fail to reject' it, but you never 'accept' it. This asymmetry comes from the analogy to a presumption of innocence: the null is assumed true unless the evidence is strong enough to reject it. The Bayesian view is symmetric, you compute the posterior probability of each hypothesis given the data, with no privileged null. The classical approach prioritizes controlling false positives (Type I) because in many scientific and regulatory contexts, a false discovery is considered more costly than a missed detection. This is a choice about error costs, not a mathematical necessity.

title: McNemar test: I do not understand why (or how, or when?) it works
attempt: The McNemar test is for paired binary data, when each subject is measured twice (e.g., before and after an intervention) and the outcome is binary. It tests whether the proportion of successes is the same at the two time points. The key insight is that it focuses on the DISCORDANT pairs, the subjects whose outcome changed. The 2x2 table of before/after has four cells: (success,success), (success,failure), (failure,success), (failure,failure). The concordant cells (success,success) and (failure,failure) provide no information about change. The McNemar test statistic is (b-c)^2/(b+c), where b and c are the two discordant cells. Under the null of no change, b and c should be equal (changes are equally likely in either direction), so the statistic follows a chi-square distribution with 1 df. It works because it conditions on the number of subjects who changed and tests whether the changes are symmetric.
